learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the restless nature of the sea! Learn the difference between the surface rippling of waves, the daily rise and fall of tides, and the massive rivers of ocean currents.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Waves are actually energy moving across the water surface, driven by the wind. The water itself mostly bobs up and down in a circular motion; it does not travel forward with the wave!
Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, primarily caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun. The moon has a stronger effect because it is much closer to Earth.

When the Sun, Moon, and Earth align in a straight line (Full Moon or New Moon), their combined gravity creates massive 'Spring Tides'. When the Sun and Moon are at a 90-degree angle, we get weaker 'Neap Tides'.

Currents are massive 'rivers' of water flowing consistently in a specific direction through the ocean. Warm currents flow from the equator towards the poles. Cold currents bring freezing water from the poles towards the equator.

fun_activity.title: 🌔 The Gravity Tow
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine wearing a loose, oversized t-shirt. If a friend stands in front of you and pulls the front of your shirt, it bulges towards them. The Moon acts like your friend, pulling the Earth's loose 'water shirt' towards it, creating a high tide bulge!

exam_tips: 📌 Waves transfer ENERGY, not water mass. Tides are vertical movements of water. Currents are horizontal movements of water.
📌 The meeting place of warm and cold ocean currents (e.g., where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current) produces thick fog but creates the best fishing grounds in the world.
📌 Ocean currents are largely driven by prevailing winds, differences in water density, and the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force).
quick_recap: ⭐ Wind is the primary driving force behind ocean waves.
⭐ The Moon exerts a stronger tide-generating force than the Sun due to its proximity to Earth.
⭐ Ocean currents act like global conveyor belts, modifying the climate of coastal regions.
